To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV infection is unique, that it is more common in women in sub-Saharan Africa and that there are important psychological implications for the women, their partners and their families.

the prevalence of HIV in pregnant women is 0.2% in England and Wales, but is 4-6% in some parts of Africa, that the majority of infected women are young, that most infected women have had a sexually transmitted infection, that most women with HIV infection do not transmit it to their babies, that the risk of transmission can be greatly reduced by antiretroviral therapy, and that women with HIV infection have the same pregnancy outcomes as other women.

the prevalence of HIV in women attending antenatal clinics in South Africa is low, that the risk of HIV infection in women attending antanatal clinics is low, that there is no evidence to suggest that women who attend antenatal clinics are more likely to be HIV infected than women who do not attend antenatal clinic, and that there is no significant difference in the prevalence of HIV infection in pregnant women who have had a previous pregnancy and those who are having their first pregnancy.

the epidemiology of HIV infection in women and the social and psychological impact of HIV infection in pregnant women.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is an urgent need to develop a comprehensive approach to care of HIV positive women.
HIV is a serious problem which will continue to affect women and their children in the foreseeable future.
the HIV epidemic has a major impact on women's health and that women's health has a major impact of the HIV epidemic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of infection in the antenatal population is very low and the number of babies born HIV positive is also low.
the prevalence is high in sub-Saharan Africa.
HIV in women is increasing in prevalence, is a major health problem in developing countries, is difficult to manage and requires a multidisciplinary approach to management.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have to be more aggressive in our testing, and more aggressive in our counseling.
the HIV/AIDS epidemic is a complex phenomenon that is not limited to the medical aspects.
we need to do better in terms of the care we provide to women with HIV.
